newsitem.title: USA: EIA outlook for U.S. oil production.
newsitem.headline: EIA outlook for U.S. oil production.

text.p: U.S. crude oil production in 1996 should be more robust than first expected, with output in the lower-48 states holding at 5.08 million barrels per day instead of falling to 5.01 million bpd, the Energy Information Administration said on Monday.
Total U.S. production should fall by 1.4 percent to 6.47 million bpd in 1996 from 1995, EIA said in its latest short-term energy outlook, revising its earlier forecast of a 2.6 percent decline.
EIA projected output in 1997 would drop 2.3 percent to 6.32 million bpd, instead of falling to 6.16 million bpd.

The higher-than-expected production should stem growth in crude oil imports, which were seen reaching 7.42 million bpd in 1996 and 7.83 million bpd in 1997, or 20,000 to 40,000 bpd less than in EIA's June forecast.
The outlook for total petroleum imports -- crude and products -- was similarly revised down to 8.5 million bpd in 1996 and 8.88 million bpd in 1997.
U.S. demand for petroleum products was expected to increase 2.3 percent to 18.12 million bpd in 1996, a slightly stronger rate of growth than previously predicted.

But EIA saw petroleum demand in 1997 growing by only 1.0 percent to 18.31 million bpd, assuming that U.S. economic growth would slow to 2.0 percent in 1997 from 2.4 percent this year and the upcoming winter would be milder than last winter.
EIA lowered its outlook for gasoline demand growth in 1996 to 1.0 percent from 1.3 percent largely because of "weaker-than-expected summer demand."
Total gasoline demand is expected to be 7.87 million bpd in 1996 and 8.08 million bpd in 1997.
"Refineries are reporting very little growth in shipments," an EIA analyst said.
Miles traveled increased by only 1.7 percent at a time of robust economic growth, he said.
Slower economic growth and airplane fuel efficiency gains are expected to hold down growth in jet fuel demand in 1997, the analyst said.
EIA saw jet fuel demand climbing 4.0 percent in 1996 to 1.57 million bpd, but rising only 1.3 percent in 1997 to 1.59 million bpd.
For 1996, distillate demand should climb 3.4 percent to 3.32 million bpd because of the harsh weather last winter, and rise by only 0.6 percent to 3.34 million bpd in 1997.
Residual fuel demand for 1996 was pegged at 850,000 bpd, unchanged from last year, and rising 2.4 percent in 1997 to 870,000 bpd, less than earlier forecast.
